newsitem.title: FRANCE: Protesters march against French immigration bill.
newsitem.headline: Protesters march against French immigration bill.

text.p: French intellectuals, artists and left-wing politicians led tens of thousands of demonstrators through Paris on Saturday in a march against a conservative government bill to stiffen a crackdown on illegal immigration.

"We all are children of immigrants," chanted the protesters, some of whom carried suitcases with the words "Whose turn now?" -- a reference to expulsions of illegal foreign residents and far-rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen's calls to send all aliens home.
Organisers said 150,000 had taken in the march, seen as a test of public feeling over the ideological battle in which each side accuses the other of playing into the hands of Le Pen's National Front.
Police estimated the number at 33,000. There were small marches in several other cities. The ruling Gaullist RPR party called the protests "a stinging failure".

As an opinion poll showed a majority of French voters backed the bill, young Gaullists handed out in various cities leaflets saying the protests no longer had any reason since the bill's most controversial clause had been removed.

But the dispute over the excised clause -- that would have obliged French hosts to notify the police when foreign guests from developing countries left their homes -- has turned into a wider battle over a four-year-old crackdown on immigration.

Former president Francois Mitterrand's widow Danielle and film star Emmanuelle Beart took part in the march called by "121 names difficult to pronounce" -- personalities of foreign descent quoting from a poem by Louis Aragon on foreigners shot by the Nazis for joining in the World War Two French Resistance.
Children carried a "Foreigners are our friends" banner.

Some protesters carried portraits of French collaborationist leader Marshal Philippe Petain, saying the bill's excised clause recalled his World War Two order to denounce Jews. The march began at the Gare de l'Est station from where Jews were deported to Nazi death camps.

Hundreds of Asians occupied the Saint-Jean Baptiste catholic church in Paris's heavily immigrant Belleville district to demand residence rights. Police last August ejected dozens of Africans, some of them on a hunger strike, from another Paris church they were occupying to press similar demands.

"The whole approach to immigration must be reviewed," said Gerard Mordillat, one of film-makers spearheading a call to disobey the bill made after the National Front won control of a fourth southern town, Vitrolles, in a municipal election.
Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre, accompanying President Jacques Chirac on an official visit to Bucharest, said he was determined to push his bill through parliament.
"It is by fighting illegal immigration that we will force racism and xenophobia to retreat," he told reporters.
The battle raged in newspapers as well as on the street.
The influential Le Monde said the crackdown on immigration and the rise of the National Front were being seen abroad as signs of a mounting xenophobia harming France's image.

The conservative daily Le Figaro, accusing intellectuals of being irresponsible in denying authorities the means to control illegal immigration, published a survey commissioned by the government showing 67 percent of voters backed the revised bill.
The Sofres opinion poll said 61 percent of 1,000 voters questioned opposed the call for civil disobedience.
The dispute has embarrassed the main Socialist opposition party, wary of alienating those working-class voters who blame immigration for contributing to acute unemployment.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin sent lieutenants to the Paris protest, preferring to march more discreetly in Toulouse.
He said the bill was repressive and inefficient and the Socialists would repeal it if they won power in 1998 elections.
More protests are planned for Tuesday when the bill is due for its final reading in the National Assembly.

The Assembly's legislation committeee, in a bid to rescue the bill, passed an amendment last Thursday making foreigners on short-term visas, rather than their French hosts, responsible for reporting their own departure to the authorities.

While civil rights groups, intellectuals and trade unions call for a softening of immigration regulations, Le Pen wants them further stiffened and French and European nationals to be given preference in jobs, housing and family allowances.
